sentences.text: It took her two weeks to get the materials.
She used her allowance and the money she had saved from her birthday.
She bought foam board at the art store on Belmont, and a metal ruler, and thin balsa wood that was easier to cut than she had expected.
She bought good glue and small tweezers and a package of tiny plastic figures the size of her fingernail, meant for architects who wanted to show a person in their models for scale.
She cleared her desk and taped a large piece of paper to it.
She had decided she would build the whole house at one-fiftieth scale, which meant a real room ten feet wide would be about two and a half inches in her model.
She wrote that at the top of the paper.
She wrote her mother's name too, small, in the corner.
And then she opened the sketchbook to the first page, and she began.
The first room she built was the curved-wall room from page two.
It was harder than she had expected.
Foam board did not like to curve.
She had to score it, again and again, with the back of her knife, until it would bend without cracking.
She got it wrong the first time and threw the whole thing away.
She got it wrong the second time and cried a little in the bathroom so her father would not see.
On the third try, it curved.
When it was standing on her desk, small and honest and slightly wobbly, she went back to the sketchbook.
The note in the margin said: A curved wall makes people slow down.
They cannot walk straight across it.
This is good in a kitchen.
It is bad in a hallway.
Bea thought about that.
She thought her mother must have watched people walking through rooms and noticed things.
She wondered if that was the sort of thing you were born knowing, or if you learned it.
She worked on it every day for the rest of June and most of July.
Her father asked her, more than once, if she wanted help.
She always said no.
She was not sure why.
It felt like the sort of thing she needed to do alone.
Or maybe not quite alone — she was doing it with the sketchbook, and the sketchbook felt, sometimes, like a very quiet person sitting next to her.
The rooms began to line up on the shelf above her desk.
The spiral staircase, made from thin balsa strips glued to a paper tube.
The library with the glass ceiling, which she made from a piece of clear plastic she cut from a strawberry container.
The kitchen with the folding table, whose hinge she made from a bent paperclip.
The rooftop garden with tiny paper trees, each one no bigger than a grain of rice.
Every time she finished one, she read the note in the margin, and she wrote the note on a small card, and she taped the card to the room.
She began to know things about her mother that she had not known before.
Her mother thought children should have their own doors.
Every room she designed for a child had a small second door, low to the floor.
"So they can leave when they need to," she had written.
"And so they can come back in without asking."
Her mother hated corridors.
"A corridor is space that has been wasted," one note said.
"If you must have one, make it a room.
Put a window in it.
Put a chair in it.
Give it a reason to exist."
Her mother liked ceilings that were low in some places and high in others.
She thought this was truer to how people actually wanted to feel.
"You are cozy where the ceiling is low," she wrote.
"You breathe where it is high."
Bea began to think that if she had known her mother longer, they might have agreed on a lot of things.
By the last week of July, she had built twenty-nine of the forty-two rooms.
She had one to go before the very last one, and she had been saving it because she was a little afraid of it.
It was the room on the second-to-last page, and it did not have any furniture drawn in.
It was very small, and shaped like a corner, and it had a round window and a low door.
In the margin, her mother had written just three words: For a small one.
